entries.label: discourse marker
entries.meaning: Starts a sentence to get the listener's attention before you state your view firmly, often to settle a disagreement.
entries.usage: Used at the start of a sentence, followed by a short pause: *Look, I know you're upset, but …* It signals that you are about to be direct, so it can sound impatient or defensive if you use it often. Managers and public figures use it to sound frank and in control.
examples: **Look**, I know you're upset, but yelling at me won't fix the car.
**Look**, we can't afford a new kitchen this year. Let's paint the cabinets and wait.
**Look**, if you don't want to come, just say so. I won't be offended.

drill.sentence: {{Look}}, I'm not trying to tell you how to raise your kids. I'm just worried about him.
drill.hint: one-word attention-getter before a frank point (not *listen*)

entries.related: *listen* — works the same way; *see* — introduces an explanation: *See, the problem is …*; *here's the thing* — introduces the key problem.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Added after a statement to show that you believed it at the time, but it turned out to be wrong.
entries.usage: Common in storytelling, spoken and written, usually at the end of a sentence for a small comic or dramatic twist: *The test was easy, or so I thought.* The next sentence normally reveals what really happened. *Or so we thought* and *or so it seemed* work the same way.
examples: The hike would take two hours, **or so I thought**. We got back after dark.
My new roommate was quiet and tidy, **or so I thought**. Then his band moved in.
The sale was done, **or so we thought**, until the buyer's bank pulled out.

drill.sentence: The dog was safely in the backyard, {{or so I thought}}. Then I saw him chasing the mail truck.
drill.hint: that was my belief, but I was wrong (not *seemed*)

entries.related: *or so it seemed* — same twist, less personal; *little did I know* — dramatic, introduces what you didn't know; *as it turns out* — reveals the real result.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Means something similar to what was just said, when you can't or don't need to be exact.
entries.usage: Very common as *something along those lines* at the end of a sentence, when you remember the general idea but not the exact words or details. It also asks for similar ideas: *anything along those lines*. It's fine in speech and in work emails; *along the same lines* is used to add a similar point.
examples: "What did the doctor say?" "Rest, drink lots of fluids, **something along those lines**."
We're looking for a gift for my dad, maybe a watch or something **along those lines**.
If you have ideas **along those lines**, send them to me before Friday.

drill.sentence: I don't remember her exact words, but she said she was 'done with this town,' or something {{along those lines}}.
drill.hint: similar to that (not *like that* or *to that effect*)

entries.related: *something like that* — more casual; *along the same lines* — adds a similar point; *or something* — vaguer, very casual.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A sarcastic reply meaning that you don't believe what someone said at all.
entries.usage: The words are positive, but a flat or mocking tone turns them into disbelief, so it's for friends and family rather than colleagues you don't know well. It usually reacts to a claim or a promise that sounds unlikely. Said quickly and sincerely, *yeah, right* can also just confirm something, so tone matters.
examples: "I'll start going to the gym every morning." "**Yeah, right**. You said that in January."
"The landlord says the heat will be fixed by tonight." "**Yeah, right**."
He told his boss the email went to spam. **Yeah, right**.

drill.sentence: "Don't worry, I'll pay you back next week." "{{Yeah, right}}. You still owe me from last summer."
drill.hint: sarcastic: I don't believe that at all (not *if you say so* or anything with *sure*)

entries.related: *if you say so* — doubtful but not mocking; *sure you will* — sarcastic about a promise; *I wouldn't count on it* — it probably won't happen.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A skeptical or noncommittal reply: you're not sure something will happen, and you won't decide or promise now.
entries.usage: Parents famously use it to avoid saying *no* to children, and adults use it about plans or predictions they doubt, such as a friend's promise to change. The tone can be hopeful, neutral or openly doubtful. Because it avoids commitment, it can frustrate someone who wants a clear answer.
examples: "Can we go to the zoo this weekend?" "**We'll see**, sweetie."
The new coach says we'll make the playoffs this year. **We'll see**.
"I think the client will love the new design." "Maybe. **We'll see**."

drill.sentence: My brother says he's going to quit smoking for good this time. {{We'll see}}.
drill.hint: I doubt it, but let's wait (not *yeah, right* or *time will tell*)

entries.related: *time will tell* — neutral, we'll know later; *I doubt it* — openly skeptical; *yeah, right* — sarcastic disbelief.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Says that two outcomes are equally possible and you can't predict which one will happen.
entries.usage: Used about games, job offers, court cases, close votes and medical outcomes. It sounds neutral and careful, so sports commentators, doctors and lawyers use it a lot. A close contest can also be called *a toss-up* or *too close to call*.
examples: Both teams are healthy and playing well. Honestly, **it could go either way** on Sunday.
The doctor says the knee might heal on its own, but **it could go either way**.
The hiring committee is split between the last two candidates. **It could go either way**.

drill.sentence: The jury has been out for three days, so {{it could go either way}}.
drill.hint: both results are equally possible (not *it's a toss-up* or *anything …*)

entries.related: *a toss-up* — a situation where both outcomes are equally likely; *too close to call* — used for tight races and votes; *anything could happen* — vaguer.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: An understated way to say that you're unhappy with something, often more unhappy than the words suggest.
entries.usage: Common at work and at home when you accept something you dislike, such as a schedule change, a decision or a long visit. The understatement sounds controlled and polite, but listeners understand the displeasure. It takes a noun or an *-ing* form, and *not thrilled with* is common for results.
examples: **I'm not thrilled about** working on Christmas Eve, but someone has to.
My wife **isn't thrilled about** my brother staying with us for a month.
Investors **weren't thrilled with** the quarterly numbers, and the stock fell eight percent.

drill.sentence: {{I'm not thrilled about}} the new parking rules, but I'll follow them like everyone else.
drill.hint: unhappy with, said by understatement (not *crazy*, *happy*, *wild* or *a fan*)

entries.related: *I'm not crazy about* — I don't really like it; *I'm not happy about* — plainer, more openly negative; *I'm not sold on* — I'm not convinced yet.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Says that you aren't yet convinced that an idea, plan or product is good.
entries.usage: Common in meetings, shopping and planning, followed by a noun or an *-ing* form: *I'm not sold on the color.* It suggests that better arguments could still persuade you, so it's softer than *I don't like it*. The positive *I'm sold* means you're fully convinced.
examples: **I'm not sold on** the new layout. Can we see one more version?
**I'm not sold on** buying a house so far from the city. Convince me.
My husband still **isn't sold on** the idea of getting a dog.

drill.sentence: The salesman kept pushing the extended warranty, but I still {{wasn't sold on}} it.
drill.hint: not yet persuaded it was worth it (not *keen on* or *crazy about*)

entries.related: *I'm not convinced* — more formal; *I'm sold* — fully convinced; *I'm on the fence* — undecided.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Says that a proposal or a result is acceptable to you, even if it isn't ideal.
entries.usage: Common in negotiations and planning, as a reply to a compromise about a price, a date or a change. It sounds reasonable and slightly reluctant, so it means *okay* rather than *great*. *I can live with that* is equally common and a bit more definite.
examples: "How about you get the car on weekends and I take it on weekdays?" "**I could live with that**."
The hotel's a bit far from the beach, but at that price **I can live with it**.
The tiny kitchen **I could live with**, but no laundry in the building is a deal-breaker.

drill.sentence: "What if we spend Christmas with your parents and New Year's with mine?" "Okay, {{I could live with that}}."
drill.hint: that's acceptable, if not perfect (not *works for me* or *fair enough*)

entries.related: *works for me* — neutral agreement to a plan; *fair enough* — accepts something as reasonable; *I can't live with that* — I won't accept it.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A friendly, informal reply to a request, meaning *certainly, I'll do that*.
entries.usage: Common in American service jobs and among coworkers and friends: a server, a bartender or a colleague says it to agree to a request cheerfully. It's upbeat and casual, so it doesn't belong in formal emails. Don't confuse it with *you've got this* (you can do it) or *got it* (I understand).
examples: "Can I get another iced tea, please?" "**You got it**."
Whatever you need for the move, **you got it**. Just tell me when.
"Two large pizzas, one with extra cheese." "**You got it**. Twenty minutes."

drill.sentence: "Can you grab me a coffee on your way back?" "{{You got it}}. Cream and sugar?"
drill.hint: certainly, I'll do it (not *sure thing*, *you bet* or *no problem*)

entries.related: *sure thing* — very similar; *you bet* — similar, a bit more enthusiastic; *got it* — I understand; *you've got this* — encouragement: you can do it.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A friendly, informal way to say *of course* when agreeing to a request; it's also a casual reply to *thanks*.
entries.usage: Common in American speech between coworkers, neighbors, and staff and customers. It sounds relaxed and willing, a bit more casual than *of course*. As a reply to *Thanks!*, it means *you're welcome*; the noun *a sure thing* is different and means something certain to happen.
examples: "Can you water my plants while I'm away?" "**Sure thing**. Just leave me the key."
"Thanks for the ride home, Mr. Lopez!" "**Sure thing**. Tell your mom I said hi."
"Could you add me to the calendar invite?" "**Sure thing**, I'll do it now."

drill.sentence: "Can you text me when you get home?" "{{Sure thing}}. Probably around eleven."
drill.hint: a casual, willing yes, two words (not *you bet*, *will do*, *of course* or *no problem*)

entries.related: *you got it* — very similar; *of course* — more neutral; *no problem* — casual, often a reply to thanks.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Warns that what you're saying is an unfinished idea, not a firm proposal or decision.
entries.usage: Common in meetings, brainstorming and family planning, before or after a tentative idea, so that others feel free to reject it. It also protects you from being held to the idea later. *Thinking aloud* means the same and sounds a bit more formal.
examples: **I'm just thinking out loud**, but what if we moved the wedding to the fall?
**I'm just thinking out loud** here: could we split the team into two shifts?
Sorry, ignore me. **I was just thinking out loud**.

drill.sentence: "Wait, so you're quitting your job?" "No, no, {{I'm just thinking out loud}}. Nothing's decided."
drill.hint: these are unfinished ideas, not a plan (not *… aloud* or *spitballing*)

entries.related: *just spitballing* — informal, throwing out rough ideas; *off the top of my head* — without checking; *just an idea* — plainer.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Says that a topic is separate and too long to discuss now, often hinting that it's interesting.
entries.usage: Used in conversation to avoid a long side story, or to tease that there's more to tell, often with a promise to tell it later. It also marks a second issue as harder or different: *Getting there was easy; getting back is a whole other story.* *A whole other* is informal; *a different story* sounds more neutral.
examples: We got to the airport on time. Getting back home, though? **That's a whole other story**.
"How did you two meet?" "Oh, that's **a whole other story**. Remind me to tell you later."
The budget was approved. Whether we can hire anyone **is a whole other story**.

drill.sentence: Yes, I eventually got my suitcase back, but how it ended up in Peru is {{a whole other story}}.
drill.hint: a separate, long topic (not *another*, *different* or *long*)

entries.related: *long story short* — sums up a long story briefly; *a different story* — a different situation, often worse; *but I digress* — I've wandered off the topic.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Asks for someone's opinion or interpretation of something puzzling or new.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and meetings when you want help understanding a person, an event or a result: *What do you make of the new manager?* It sounds open and curious and invites a thoughtful answer. The answer *I don't know what to make of it* means you're unsure how to interpret something.
examples: **What do you make of** the new neighbors? They seem a bit cold.
She replied to my long message with just 'k.' **What do you make of** that?
**What do you make of** these sales numbers? Up in March, down in April.

drill.sentence: {{What do you make of}} all those police cars outside the bank this morning?
drill.hint: how do you interpret (not *… think of* or *… think about*)

entries.related: *what do you think of* — asks for an opinion, more general; *I don't know what to make of it* — I'm unsure how to interpret it; *how do you read* — similar, more analytical.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Says that you can't decide between two options because both have strong arguments.
entries.usage: Common when weighing personal choices, often followed by *between A and B* or *about* + topic. It signals real inner conflict, more than *I'm not sure*. Said in a discussion, it also invites advice: *I'm torn, what would you do?*
entries.pattern: I'm torn (between A and B / about something)
examples: **I'm torn** between the job in Seattle and staying near my family.
**I'm torn about** whether to move my dad into assisted living.
"Pasta or steak?" "**I'm torn**. Everything looks good."

drill.sentence: I love both apartments, so {{I'm torn}}. One has a view, and the other is ten minutes from work.
drill.hint: pulled between two options (not *can't decide* or *on the fence*)

entries.related: *I'm on the fence* — undecided, often less emotional; *I'm of two minds* — same, a bit more formal; *I'm having second thoughts* — I'm doubting a decision I've already made.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A reply meaning that you agree completely with what was just said.
entries.usage: Used warmly or with a sigh, usually after a complaint or a strong opinion. It's informal and slightly old-fashioned but still common, and it doesn't ask the person to repeat anything. *Tell me about it* and *You're telling me* are similar.
examples: "That was the longest meeting of my life." "**You can say that again**."
"Rent in this city is insane." "**You can say that again**. Mine went up three hundred."
"Your grandmother makes the best pie." "Oh, **you can say that again**."

drill.sentence: "This line is taking forever." "{{You can say that again}}. We've been standing here for forty minutes."
drill.hint: I completely agree (not *tell me about it*, *telling me* or *I know, right*)

entries.related: *tell me about it* — agrees, often about a shared problem; *you're telling me* — agrees strongly, from experience; *I couldn't agree more* — more formal.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Introduces a related point because the conversation is already about that topic.
entries.usage: Used in meetings and conversation to raise something connected before the topic changes, often as *while we're on the subject of* + noun. It sounds natural and efficient. *Speaking of which* is shorter and more casual.
entries.pattern: while we're on the subject (of + noun), …
examples: **While we're on the subject** of money, you still owe me twenty bucks.
**While we're on the subject**, has anyone booked a place for the holiday party?
"The kids need new shoes." "**While we're on the subject**, Emma's coat is too small too."

drill.sentence: {{While we're on the subject}} of vacations, did you ever decide where you're going in June?
drill.hint: as the topic has already come up (five words; not *speaking …*)

entries.related: *speaking of (which)* — shorter and more casual; *on a related note* — adds a connected point, a bit more formal; *while I have you* — raises a point while the person is there.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A skeptical question that challenges a claim, asking when it became true and often implying that it isn't.
entries.usage: Said with surprise or irritation when someone states a new rule, habit or fact you doubt. It can stand alone or start a question: *Since when do you like jazz?* It sounds challenging, so outside close relationships it can come across as rude.
examples: "I don't eat sugar anymore." "**Since when**? You had cake yesterday."
**Since when** do we need a permit to put up a fence?
**Since when** is it okay to show up an hour late to a meeting?

drill.sentence: "Dad says we're not allowed to use our phones at dinner." "{{Since when}}? He's always on his."
drill.hint: skeptical: that's a new rule? (not *says who* or *really*)

entries.related: *says who?* — challenges the authority behind a claim; *really?* — plain surprise; *that's news to me* — I didn't know that.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: An informal way to ask someone to repeat what they said, because you didn't hear it or can't believe it.
entries.usage: Used among friends and family, often after surprising news, with a rising tone. It's casual and a bit playful, so with a client or a boss *Sorry, could you repeat that?* is safer. *Say again?* is similar, especially on the phone.
examples: "I just bought a boat." "**Come again**? You don't even swim."
**Come again**? Sorry, the music's really loud in here.
"The repair will be two thousand dollars." "**Come again**?"

drill.sentence: "We're naming the baby Thunder." "{{Come again}}? Did you just say Thunder?"
drill.hint: what did you just say?! (not *excuse me*, *pardon* or *say …*)

entries.related: *excuse me?* — can sound offended; *sorry?* — polite, when you didn't hear; *pardon?* — more formal.

entries.term: I'm not a big fan of
entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A polite, mild way to say that you don't like something.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation, reviews and meetings, because it softens a dislike: *I'm not a big fan of open offices.* It works for food, styles, habits and ideas, and also for people (*I'm not a big fan of his*), where it sounds diplomatic. The positive *I'm a big fan of* means you really like something.
examples: **I'm not a big fan of** spicy food, so I'll get the chicken.
**I'm not a big fan of** long phone calls. Can you just text me?
Honestly, **I'm not a big fan of** open offices. I can't focus with all the noise.

drill.sentence: {{I'm not a big fan of}} winter, so we're spending February in Florida with my parents.
drill.hint: I don't really like (not *crazy about*)

entries.related: *I'm not crazy about* — very similar, a bit more casual; *I can't stand* — strong dislike; *not my thing* — not to my taste.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Means that nothing more needs to be said, because the point is already clear.
entries.usage: A short reply showing that you understand completely, often after a detail that explains everything, like a famous name or a bad sign. It can also end your own remark when the conclusion is obvious. It's casual and often humorous.
examples: "The party's at Mike's, and his parents are out of town." "**Enough said**. I'm in."
"Why didn't you buy the house?" "Two words: flood zone. **Enough said**."
The restaurant got a C from the health inspector. **Enough said**.

drill.sentence: "The concert's on a school night, and it ends at midnight." "{{Enough said}}. We'll skip it."
drill.hint: the point is clear; nothing to add (not *say no more*)

entries.related: *say no more* — I understand, you don't need to explain; *need I say more?* — ends your own point with a strong hint; *I'll leave it at that* — I won't say more.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: In my opinion, judged by my own standards.
entries.usage: Used in conversation to state a personal judgment firmly, often about values: *In my book, being on time is basic respect.* It can start or end a sentence. It sounds informal and a bit folksy, so avoid it in formal writing.
examples: Anyone who tips less than fifteen percent is cheap **in my book**.
**In my book**, a good boss is someone who admits their mistakes.
She drove four hours to help me move. That makes her a hero **in my book**.

drill.sentence: {{In my book}}, if you borrow someone's car, you bring it back with a full tank.
drill.hint: by my personal standards (not *personally*, *if you ask me* or *in my opinion*)

entries.related: *if you ask me* — offers an opinion, often a critical one; *in my opinion* — neutral, fine in writing; *by my standards* — plainer.

entries.term: when all is said and done
entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Introduces what matters most or what will be true in the end, after everything has been considered.
entries.usage: Used in conversation, speeches and writing to sum up after a long discussion or a complicated situation. It means much the same as *at the end of the day* but sounds a little more formal. It usually starts the sentence or comes after *but*.
examples: **When all is said and done**, he's still your father, and he loves you.
We'll argue about the details, but **when all is said and done**, the kitchen will look great.
**When all is said and done**, the merger cost far more than anyone predicted.

drill.sentence: We had our fights, but {{when all is said and done}}, those were the best years of my life.
drill.hint: once everything is considered (not *at the end of the day*, *in the end* or *all things considered*)

entries.related: *at the end of the day* — same, more informal; *ultimately* — one word, neutral; *all things considered* — after thinking about every factor.

entries.term: not to change the subject, but …
entries.spoken_term: not to change the subject, but
entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A polite way to introduce a new topic that has little to do with the current one.
entries.usage: Used in conversation and meetings to show you know you're switching topics, which makes the shift less abrupt. It's often a little humorous, because people say it exactly when they are changing the subject. For a closely related topic, *speaking of which* fits better.
examples: **Not to change the subject, but** did anyone feed the cat this morning?
**Not to change the subject, but** is that a new car in your driveway?
**Not to change the subject, but** we only have ten minutes left, and we haven't discussed the budget.

drill.sentence: {{Not to change the subject, but}} are you guys hungry? I saw a great taco truck outside.
drill.hint: politely moving to a new topic (not *by the way* or *on a different note*)

entries.related: *on a different note* — switches topics, a bit more formal; *by the way* — adds a side point casually; *speaking of which* — moves to a related topic.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Introduces something you want to say right away so that you don't forget to say it.
entries.usage: Common in conversations, phone calls and emails, often to add a practical detail such as a date, a payment or a message from someone. It sounds friendly and natural, and it can interrupt the current topic without seeming rude. It usually starts the sentence and is followed by a comma.
examples: **Before I forget**, your mom called and wants you to call her back.
**Before I forget**, here's the twenty dollars I owe you.
**Before I forget**, the office will be closed on Monday for the holiday.

drill.sentence: {{Before I forget}}, the plumber's coming at eight tomorrow, so someone needs to be home.
drill.hint: so it doesn't slip my mind (not *by the way* or *while I think of it*)

entries.related: *by the way* — adds a side point casually; *while I think of it* — same, a bit less common; *just so you know* — gives information neutrally.

entries.term: I never thought of it that way
entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Says that someone's view is new to you and makes you see the matter differently.
entries.usage: A friendly, open-minded reply in discussions at home or at work, often with *Huh* or *Wow* before it. It shows real interest and can soften a disagreement. Common variants are *I hadn't thought of it that way* and *I never looked at it that way*.
examples: "Renting means you never have to fix the roof." "Huh, **I never thought of it that way**."
**I'd never thought of it that way**, but you're right: my commute is my only quiet time.
My therapist said anger is often fear in disguise. **I never thought of it that way**.

drill.sentence: "Losing that job might be the push you needed to start your own business." "Wow, {{I never thought of it that way}}."
drill.hint: that view is new to me (not *when you put it …* or *… looked at …*)

entries.related: *when you put it that way* — your phrasing changes my view; *good point* — agrees with an argument; *that's one way to look at it* — polite doubt.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Says that any option is fine with you, so the other person should choose what suits them.
entries.usage: An easygoing reply when someone asks you to pick a time, a place or a method. Said warmly, it's generous; said flatly, it can sound as if you don't care. *Whatever works* on its own can also accept someone's unusual habit or method.
examples: "Should I come at six or seven?" "**Whatever works for you**. I'm home all evening."
We can talk by phone or video, **whatever works for you**.
He studies with the TV on. Strange, but **whatever works**.

drill.sentence: "Is it okay if I pay you back in two parts?" "Sure, {{whatever works for you}}."
drill.hint: any option suits me, you choose (not *up to you* or *your call*)

entries.related: *up to you* — you decide; *your call* — the decision is yours; *I'm flexible* — I can adapt to any option.

entries.term: you can't make this stuff up
entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Says that something is so strange or absurd that nobody could have invented it, so it must be true.
entries.usage: Said with amusement or disbelief before or after telling a bizarre true story about news, family or work. It's casual and often a little gleeful. *You can't make this up* is a shorter form, and *you couldn't make it up* is the usual British version.
examples: The fire station burned down because someone left the stove on. **You can't make this stuff up**.
**You can't make this stuff up**: our wedding photographer went to the wrong wedding.
"The thief left his phone at the scene?" "With his selfies on it. **You can't make this stuff up**."

drill.sentence: The city spent ten thousand dollars on signs that say 'Don't waste money.' {{You can't make this stuff up}}.
drill.hint: this is too absurd to be invented (not *go figure*)

entries.related: *truth is stranger than fiction* — the same idea as a set saying; *go figure* — reacts to something illogical; *you couldn't make it up* — the British version.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Introduces something you're proud of, while jokingly pretending that you're not boasting.
entries.usage: Used among friends and family, usually with a smile, because everyone knows you are in fact bragging. It suits small, fun achievements: a high score, a good deal, a perfect cake. For serious achievements or at work it can sound arrogant, and *I'm proud to say* is safer.
examples: **Not to brag, but** I beat my son at chess three times in a row.
**Not to brag, but** I got these boots for half price.
My tomatoes are the biggest on the block, **not to brag**.

drill.sentence: {{Not to brag, but}} I finished the half marathon twenty minutes faster than last year.
drill.hint: half-joking intro to boasting (not *proud* or *no big deal*)

entries.related: *humblebrag* — a boast hidden in a complaint or a modest remark; *I'm proud to say* — sincere, not joking; *no big deal, but* — pretends something impressive is minor.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Warns the listener that an idea, question or request is unusual before you say it.
entries.usage: Used in casual conversation to make an odd question less awkward and to show you know it's odd. It sounds friendly and a little self-conscious. *This might sound strange, but* is more neutral, and *This might sound unusual, but* is safer at work.
examples: **This might sound weird, but** do you want to swap seats? I get carsick in the back.
**This might sound weird, but** I actually enjoy doing my taxes.
**This might sound weird, but** I think our cat actually likes the vacuum cleaner.

drill.sentence: {{This might sound weird, but}} have we met before? You look really familiar.
drill.hint: warning: my question is unusual (not *… random* or *… strange*)

entries.related: *this is random, but* — introduces an unrelated question; *don't take this the wrong way* — warns of possible offense; *I know this sounds crazy, but* — stronger.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Says that you're pleased about someone's success or brave decision; with a flat tone, it can be sarcastic.
entries.usage: Said warmly to praise an achievement or a choice, especially a hard one like quitting smoking or asking for a raise. Said flatly to someone who is boasting, it means you're not impressed. *Good for him* and *good for them* work the same way.
examples: "I finally told my boss I need more help." "**Good for you**! That took guts."
She went back to school at fifty-five. **Good for her**.
"I don't need anyone's help." "Well, **good for you**."

drill.sentence: "I quit smoking two months ago." "{{Good for you}}! That's not easy."
drill.hint: well done, I'm happy for you (not *way to go*, *congrats* or *… job*)

entries.related: *way to go* — enthusiastic praise; *I'm happy for you* — warmer, more personal; *congratulations* — for big events.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A polite, indirect way to ask for something or to make an invitation.
entries.usage: The past continuous makes the request softer than *Can you …?*, so it's common with people you don't know well, with bosses and in emails. It is followed by statement word order, not question order: *I was wondering if you could help me.* *I was wondering whether* is a bit more formal.
entries.pattern: I was wondering if + subject + could / would / verb
examples: **I was wondering if** you could watch the dog this weekend. I'll make you dinner.
Hi, **I was wondering if** you have any tables free for Saturday night.
**I was wondering if** we could move our call to Thursday afternoon.

drill.sentence: Hi, Mr. Lee. {{I was wondering if}} I could leave a little early today for a dentist appointment.
drill.hint: polite indirect request, past continuous (not *do you mind* or *I was hoping*)

mistake.wrong: I was wondering if could you send me the file.
mistake.right: I was wondering if you could send me the file.
mistake.why: After *I was wondering if*, use statement word order: the subject comes before the verb.

entries.related: *I was hoping* — similar, a bit more personal; *would you mind* — asks for an action; *do you happen to* — asks about knowledge or things.

entries.term: let's not get ahead of ourselves
entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Warns that it's too early to act or celebrate, because a necessary earlier step hasn't happened yet.
entries.usage: Used to calm excitement in meetings, sports and family plans, for example when someone plans how to spend money that hasn't arrived. It sounds sensible and slightly cautious, rarely rude. *Don't get ahead of yourself* says the same to one person and can sound more critical.
examples: "We could put a pool in the backyard!" "**Let's not get ahead of ourselves**. We haven't bought the house yet."
We won one game. **Let's not get ahead of ourselves** and start talking about the playoffs.
The first interview went well, but **let's not get ahead of ourselves**.

drill.sentence: "Should we start looking at wedding venues?" "{{Let's not get ahead of ourselves}}. We've been dating for three weeks."
drill.hint: it's too early for that (not *slow down*, *one step …* or *… rush …*)

entries.related: *don't count your chickens before they hatch* — don't assume success too early; *one step at a time* — deal with things in order; *jump the gun* — act too early.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Asks to avoid a topic because it would cause an argument, pain or embarrassment.
entries.usage: Used in conversation, with a smile or a firm tone, when someone mentions a sensitive subject such as an ex, money or an old fight. It's softer than *I don't want to talk about it* and suggests both people know why. *Don't go there* is blunter and can be a warning.
examples: "Remember your ex's birthday party?" "Oh, **let's not go there**."
If you bring up the inheritance at dinner, it'll start a fight. **Let's not go there**.
"So how much did the renovation really cost?" "**Let's not go there**."

drill.sentence: "Why did you and your brother stop speaking?" "{{Let's not go there}}. Can we talk about something else?"
drill.hint: I want to avoid that topic (not *don't ask* or *rather not*)

entries.related: *don't go there* — blunter, can be a warning; *I'd rather not talk about it* — plainer; *don't ask* — it's a bad story I won't tell.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Says that you're starting to doubt a decision you've already made or agreed to.
entries.usage: Common about big personal choices such as a wedding, a move, a purchase or a job offer. It's often followed by *about* + noun or *-ing*. It signals that you might change your mind, so it often starts a careful conversation.
entries.pattern: have second thoughts (about something / doing something)
examples: **I'm having second thoughts** about the move. My parents are getting older.
She signed the lease, but now she's **having second thoughts**.
Now that the forecast says snow, half the group **is having second thoughts** about the camping trip.

drill.sentence: I already paid the deposit for the puppy, but {{I'm having second thoughts}}. Our apartment is tiny.
drill.hint: I'm starting to doubt my decision (not *cold feet*)

entries.related: *get cold feet* — suddenly feel nervous about a big step; *on second thought* — I've just changed my mind; *I'm torn* — I can't decide between two options.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Said after a hopeful remark to avoid bad luck, as if saying it aloud could spoil your good fortune.
entries.usage: Said right after a statement about good luck, health or safety so far. Many people actually tap a table or their head while saying it, often half-jokingly. It's the American form; British speakers say *touch wood*.
examples: The car's never broken down, **knock on wood**.
**Knock on wood**, the baby's been sleeping through the night for a week now.
We haven't had a single injury this season, **knock on wood**.

drill.sentence: My laptop is seven years old and still runs fine, {{knock on wood}}.
drill.hint: said to avoid bad luck (not *touch …* or *fingers crossed*)

entries.related: *touch wood* — British version; *fingers crossed* — hoping for future luck; *I don't want to jinx it* — I won't say it, to avoid bad luck.

entries.term: I don't want to jinx it
entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Says that you won't talk about a hoped-for result, because talking about it might bring bad luck.
entries.usage: Used half seriously about job offers, pregnancies, games and deals that are going well but aren't certain. It's a reason to stay quiet, or to stop someone from celebrating too early. Sports fans also accuse each other: *Don't say it, you'll jinx it!*
examples: **I don't want to jinx it**, but I think this might be the year our team finally wins.
"Are you guys going to win the championship?" "**I don't want to jinx it**."
We might have a buyer for the house, but **I don't want to jinx it** by telling everyone.

drill.sentence: Things with the new guy are going great, but {{I don't want to jinx it}}, so I'm not saying anything yet.
drill.hint: I fear that talking about it brings bad luck (not *get my hopes up*)

entries.related: *knock on wood* — said to avoid bad luck after a hopeful remark; *I don't want to get my hopes up* — I don't want to be disappointed; *fingers crossed* — hoping for luck.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Says that you made a mistake, understand it, and won't repeat it.
entries.usage: A short, often humorous comment after a small mistake or a bad experience, like a stolen bike or a bad sunburn. It sounds mature and light, not dramatic. At work, *lessons learned* is also a noun for a review of what went wrong on a project.
examples: I left my bike unlocked for five minutes, and it was gone. **Lesson learned**.
Cheap shoes for a twelve-hour shift? My feet were killing me. **Lesson learned**.
We launched the app without testing it on older phones. **Lesson learned**.

drill.sentence: I tried to save money with a six a.m. flight, and I was miserable all day. {{Lesson learned}}.
drill.hint: I won't make that mistake again (not *never again*)

entries.related: *never again* — stronger, often emotional; *live and learn* — mistakes teach you, a set saying; *learn the hard way* — learn from a painful experience.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Says that you've had the same experience, usually a difficult one, so you understand.
entries.usage: A short, sympathetic reply among friends and coworkers that shows solidarity rather than advice. It's often extended to *Been there, done that*, which can also mean you're bored with something because you've already done it. *Anyone who's been there* refers to people with the same experience.
examples: "My toddler screamed through the whole flight." "Oh, **been there**. It's the worst."
"I just failed my driving test again." "**Been there**. Third time's the charm."
Any parent who's **been there** knows how hard the first week of day care is.

drill.sentence: "I sent a text complaining about my boss... to my boss." "Ugh, {{been there}}. Did she say anything?"
drill.hint: I've had that same experience (not *me too* or *same*)

entries.related: *been there, done that* — I've done it; also, I'm bored with it; *I feel you* — slang, I understand; *welcome to the club* — the same bad thing happened to me.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Says, with wry humor, that the same bad or annoying thing has happened to you too.
entries.usage: A sympathetic but joking reply when someone shares a common problem, such as no sleep as a new parent, a rejection or gray hair. It makes the person feel less alone, but it can sound dismissive if their problem is serious. *Join the club* means the same.
examples: "I haven't slept more than four hours since the baby was born." "**Welcome to the club**."
"My flight got delayed again." "**Welcome to the club**. Mine's been delayed three times."
Gray hair at thirty? **Welcome to the club**.

drill.sentence: "My kids think I'm the most embarrassing person alive." "{{Welcome to the club}}. Mine won't let me drop them off at school."
drill.hint: it happens to me too, said jokingly (not *join*)

entries.related: *join the club* — same; *been there* — I've had that experience; *you're not alone* — sincere, not joking.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Says that you're not angry or upset with someone after a conflict, a competition or a rejection.
entries.usage: Used to keep a relationship friendly after a disagreement, a lost game, a breakup or a turned-down offer. It can be a statement, or a question asking for reassurance: *No hard feelings?* It's also used to soften bad news you deliver: *No hard feelings, but we went with someone else.*
examples: You beat me fair and square. **No hard feelings**.
"Sorry I had to turn down your offer." "**No hard feelings**. Let me know if you change your mind."
We decided to go with another contractor, but **no hard feelings**. You did great work.

drill.sentence: "Are you still mad that I picked Sarah for the team?" "Not at all, {{no hard feelings}}."
drill.hint: I'm not upset with you (not *no worries* or *no harm*)

entries.related: *no harm done* — nothing bad happened; *no worries* — it's fine, very casual; *let bygones be bygones* — forget a past conflict.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Says that a mistake or accident caused no real damage, so there's no need to worry or apologize.
entries.usage: A reassuring reply to someone who apologizes for a small accident: a spilled drink, a wrong turn, a mix-up that got fixed. It's kind and relaxed, and it closes the topic. It only fits when things really turned out fine; after real damage, it sounds odd.
examples: "I'm so sorry I bumped your car!" "It's just a scratch. **No harm done**."
The kids knocked over the vase, but it didn't break, so **no harm done**.
I sent the email to the wrong person, but she deleted it. **No harm done**.

drill.sentence: "Sorry, I took your umbrella by mistake." "{{No harm done}}. It didn't even rain."
drill.hint: nothing bad happened, so it's fine (not *no worries* or *no big deal*)

entries.related: *no hard feelings* — I'm not angry with you; *no worries* — it's fine, very casual; *it's all good* — casual, everything is fine.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A comment on something surprising, ironic or illogical, meaning *try to explain that if you can*.
entries.usage: Said with a shrug after describing an unexpected or contradictory fact, usually at the end. It's casual and wry, and it suggests the thing makes little sense. Don't confuse it with *that figures*, which means the result was expected.
examples: The cheapest wine at the party got the most compliments. **Go figure**.
My son won't eat tomatoes, but he loves ketchup. **Go figure**.
"She quit the band a month before they got famous." "**Go figure**."

drill.sentence: My grandma ate bacon every day and lived to a hundred and two. {{Go figure}}.
drill.hint: that makes no sense, but there it is (not *who knew*)

entries.related: *who knew?* — pleasant surprise; *that figures* — that's what I expected; *how about that* — mild surprise.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Says that you have wandered away from your main topic, usually just before you return to it.
entries.usage: Used in conversation, talks and writing, often as *But I digress*. It sounds slightly formal and self-aware, and many people use it humorously after a long side comment. The next step is usually a return to the point: *Anyway, back to the budget.*
examples: Anyway, that's how I ended up with three cats. But **I digress**. Back to your question.
The speaker spent ten minutes on his dog, then laughed and said, "But **I digress**."
My first car didn't even have heat, but **I digress**. The point is, you don't need a new car.

drill.sentence: I once sat next to a famous chef in Paris, and he ordered a hamburger. But {{I digress}}. Let's get back to the menu.
drill.hint: I've wandered off the topic (not *anyway*)

entries.related: *anyway* — a casual way to return to the topic; *where was I?* — asks to find the topic again; *to get back to the point* — more formal.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Introduces a reason, like *because* or *since*, usually one that is obvious from the situation.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech, at the start or the end of a sentence: *Seeing as you're here, could you help me?* *Seeing as how* is a very casual variant heard mostly in American speech, and *seeing that* is a bit more formal. In academic writing, use *since* or *given that* instead.
examples: **Seeing as** you're already up, could you make the coffee?
We might as well eat out, **seeing as** the fridge is empty.
**Seeing as** the client hasn't paid, we're pausing the work.

drill.sentence: {{Seeing as}} it's your birthday, you get to pick the restaurant.
drill.hint: because, in a casual two-word form that doesn't end in *that*

entries.related: *since* — neutral, works in writing; *given that* — more formal; *now that* — because something has just changed.

entries.term: you have to hand it to (someone)
entries.spoken_term: you have to hand it to someone
entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Says that you must admit someone did something impressive, often someone you don't fully like or expected less from.
entries.usage: Used to give fair credit, often with a slightly reluctant tone. *You've got to hand it to* is equally common in speech. The achievement usually follows after a comma or a colon, or in a *for*-phrase: *You have to hand it to them for trying.*
entries.pattern: you have to / you've got to hand it to + person (for + -ing)
examples: **You have to hand it to her**: she raised three kids alone and finished her degree.
I don't like the guy, but **you've got to hand it to him**. He built that company from nothing.
**You have to hand it to the city** for fixing the potholes so fast.

drill.sentence: The restaurant looks tiny from outside, but {{you have to hand it to}} the owners: the food is incredible.
drill.hint: you must give credit to (not *give it to*)

entries.related: *give credit where credit is due* — acknowledge someone's achievement; *I'll give you that* — I admit you're right on this point; *hats off to* — praise for an achievement.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A reply showing that someone has mentioned something unpleasant you'd rather not think about.
entries.usage: Said with a groan when someone mentions a coming chore, a past embarrassment or a bill. It's humorous and friendly, not a real request to stop talking. It often comes with a reason: *Don't remind me, I still haven't started.*
examples: "Your taxes are due next week, right?" "Ugh, **don't remind me**."
"Isn't your high school reunion this weekend?" "**Don't remind me**. I still haven't lost those ten pounds."
"Is your mother-in-law still staying with you?" "**Don't remind me**. Two more weeks."

drill.sentence: "Wasn't that the night you fell into the pool at your boss's party?" "{{Don't remind me}}. I still can't look at him."
drill.hint: I'd rather not think about that (not *… ask* or *let's not go there*)

entries.related: *don't ask* — it's a bad story I won't tell; *let's not go there* — let's avoid that topic; *tell me about it* — I agree, I know that problem well.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A complaint that someone has given you useful information too late, after it could have helped.
entries.usage: Said with mock or real frustration to friends, family and coworkers, for example when they mention a sale after you've paid full price. It's usually lighthearted, but with a sharp tone it can be a real complaint. The stress falls on *now*.
examples: "That store has the same TV for two hundred dollars less." "**Now you tell me**. I bought it yesterday."
"Oh, you didn't need to bring anything." "**Now you tell me**! I baked three pies."
My coworker told me the deadline had been pushed back, after I'd worked all weekend. **Now he tells me**.

drill.sentence: "By the way, the hotel has a free shuttle from the airport." "{{Now you tell me}}! I just paid sixty dollars for a taxi."
drill.hint: that would have helped earlier! (not *thanks a lot*)

entries.related: *you could have told me earlier* — plainer and more serious; *thanks for the heads-up* — sincere thanks for a warning in time; *better late than never* — something late is still welcome.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Says that you are already dealing with a task or will start on it right away.
entries.usage: Very common at work and at home as *I'm on it* or just *On it*, in speech, chats and short emails. It sounds quick and reliable but casual, so in a formal email *I'll take care of it* is better. Said about someone else (*Mom's on it*), it reassures others that a problem is being handled.
examples: "The sink's leaking again." "**I'm on it**. Where's the wrench?"
"The client needs the revised quote by noon." "**On it**."
Don't worry about the flight change. Mom's **on it**, and she's calling the airline now.

drill.sentence: "Someone needs to order the cake for Grandpa's party." "{{I'm on it}}. I'll call the bakery tonight."
drill.hint: I'm handling that right away (not *I got it*, *I'll do it* or *leave it to me*)

entries.related: *I'll take care of it* — more formal; *leave it to me* — I'll handle it; *I got it* — casual: I'll do it, or I understand.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Gives someone permission to do something, meaning *go ahead*; it can be sincere or a little sarcastic.
entries.usage: Said sincerely to let someone use or take something, like a seat, the last cookie or your phone. Said in a dry tone, it means *go ahead, but I think it's a bad idea*. It's common in casual speech with friends, coworkers and strangers.
examples: "Mind if I take the last slice?" "**Be my guest**."
You want to call the cable company and wait on hold for an hour? **Be my guest**.
"Can I borrow your bike this weekend?" "**Be my guest**. Just lock it up."

drill.sentence: "Can I try fixing the printer myself?" "{{Be my guest}}. I've given up on it."
drill.hint: permission granted, go on (not *go ahead*, *by all means* or *knock yourself out*)

entries.related: *go ahead* — plainer permission; *help yourself* — take or use what you want, often food; *knock yourself out* — informal, go ahead, often sarcastic.
